questions.q: What is the single biggest real-world technique for preventing deadlocks?
options: Accessing objects in a consistent order across all transactions
Disabling all locking server-wide
Always using the SERIALIZABLE isolation level
Running every transaction on its own dedicated server
questions.explain: If every transaction touches the same set of rows in the same order, the cyclical wait a deadlock requires has no way to form.

questions.q: Why does keeping transactions short help reduce deadlocks?
options: The longer a lock is held after being taken, the longer the window during which a conflicting request can show up and create the conditions for a cycle
Short transactions use a different lock type entirely
Transaction length has no effect on deadlock likelihood
Short transactions automatically skip the deadlock monitor
questions.explain: Locks like exclusive locks are held until commit or rollback, so minimizing that held duration shrinks the opportunity for conflicts.

questions.q: How do helpful indexes reduce deadlock risk?
options: They let a statement locate its rows faster, and lock duration correlates with scan time, so less scanning means less lock-holding time
Indexes eliminate the need for locks entirely
Indexes only affect SELECT statements, never UPDATE or DELETE
Indexes always force table-level locking
questions.explain: A well-targeted index shrinks how much of the table must be scanned and therefore how long locks are held during that scan.

questions.q: Why is error 1205 expected to happen occasionally, even in a well-designed system?
options: Under sufficiently busy concurrent load, deadlocks can still occur even with good practices in place — it isn't automatically evidence of a bug
Error 1205 only occurs when the database is corrupted
Error 1205 means the server has run out of disk space
Error 1205 means a syntax error exists in the application code
questions.explain: Deadlocks are an expected, occasional reality of concurrent systems, which is exactly why application-level handling matters.

questions.q: What is the standard application-code response to catching error 1205 specifically?
options: Retry the same transaction from the top
Permanently disable that feature of the application
Immediately escalate to a full table lock for all future requests
Ignore the error and continue as if it committed
questions.explain: The standard retry-loop pattern catches 1205 specifically and resubmits the same transaction, since the victim's work was rolled back.
